provenance.note: Archival compilation - the legacy primary_source (Sahapedia + INTACH documentation) / secondary_sources keys and per-record `sources` citations carry the accountability. Points mark documented historic sites, not mappable extents (_location_note); the Najafgarh Jheel historic-extent polygon is a planned reconstruction task.

primary_source: Sahapedia 'Traditional Water Systems of Delhi' + INTACH Delhi chapter documentation; per-body sources below
note: Delhi's lost-water register differs from the tank cities: what vanished here is not a cascade of irrigation tanks but (1) one enormous natural lake, (2) the Mughal canal system, and (3) the tank-and-hauz network of the successive capitals. Entries are the documented, citable losses; coordinates are historic-site locations, not survey boundaries.

lost_bodies.name: Najafgarh Jheel (as a 226 sq km lake)
lost_bodies.note: The terminal lake of the Sahibi river once spread ~226 sq km; colonial and post-colonial drainage through the Najafgarh drain reduced it to a ~7 sq km remnant. The remnant survives (see flagship register); the LAKE - once Delhi's dominant water feature and flood buffer - is what was lost.
lost_bodies.location_basis: Remnant wetland on the Delhi-Haryana border

lost_bodies.name: Nahar-i-Behisht / Ali Mardan Khan's canal (city reach)
lost_bodies.note: The Mughal canal that carried Yamuna water ~130 km into Shahjahanabad, running down the centre of Chandni Chowk and through the Red Fort's Stream of Paradise. Dismantled after 1857; its alignment survives only in street names and the fort's dry marble channels.
lost_bodies.location_basis: Chandni Chowk central avenue (historic canal alignment)

lost_bodies.name: Anang Tal
lost_bodies.note: Delhi's oldest recorded tank (attributed to Anangpal Tomar II, ~1,060 CE), the water source of the first city at Lal Kot. Encroached and reduced to a pit; declared a monument of national importance in 2022, with revival attempts ongoing - a thousand-year-old tank that exists mostly as an excavation.
lost_bodies.location_basis: North of Qutb Minar complex, Mehrauli

lost_bodies.name: Hauz Rani tank
lost_bodies.note: The 'queen's tank' that served the Siri-Mehrauli corridor; the locality keeps the name but the tank itself was built over. One of the clearest cases of a Sultanate hauz surviving only as a neighbourhood name.
lost_bodies.location_basis: Hauz Rani locality, opposite Max Saket

lost_bodies.name: Satpula tank
lost_bodies.note: Firuz-era (c. 1340s) seven-arched weir-dam that impounded a tank on the Khirki stream for south Delhi's water supply and defence. The dam stands; the tank it held is gone, its bed built over - a dam without its water.

lost_bodies.name: Tughlaqabad southern reservoir
lost_bodies.note: The great bund between Tughlaqabad fort and Adilabad impounded a seasonal reservoir that was the 14th-century city's water insurance; the causeway survives as a road, the reservoir bed as settled land.

lost_bodies.name: Yamuna floodplain ox-bows and wetlands (urbanised reaches)
lost_bodies.note: The braided river's ox-bows and seasonal wetlands between Wazirabad and Okhla were progressively embanked and built over (Commonwealth Games Village, Akshardham, ISBT reaches) - the storage the 2023 flood went looking for. Wetlands International documents the NCT-wide wetland decline; the 2023 inundation map is effectively a map of this lost storage.
lost_bodies.location_basis: Representative point: eastern floodplain near the CWG Village reach

_location_note: Historic extents are not mappable as polygons from public sources; points mark documented sites. The Najafgarh Jheel historic-extent polygon (from the 1883 Gazetteer + the DPGS EMP maps) is a planned reconstruction task.
